samples: This is a command-line to-do tool that stores tasks, one per line, in a `todo.txt` file in the current directory (a missing file counts as an empty list). It supports adding a task from the remaining words, removing a task by its 1-based number (so "done" deletes the task rather than marking it), and showing the numbered list. Any unrecognized or malformed input prints a usage line, and the program needs console, environment and filesystem access. I could not tell from the code what happens if you ask to finish a number larger than the list length.

This is a command-line to-do tool that keeps its tasks, one per line, in a file called todo.txt in the current directory, and treats a missing file as an empty list. Run with "add" followed by words, it appends a task; with "done" and a number, it removes that numbered task (it deletes the task rather than marking it complete); with "show", it just lists the tasks. After an add or done it saves the file and prints the numbered list, and any other input, including a missing or non-positive number, prints a usage message. It needs only console, environment and file access, and it fails only if the file cannot be written. The code doesn't say what happens when the number is past the end of the list, so check that before relying on it.

This is a command-line to-do manager that keeps tasks one per line in a file called todo.txt in the current directory. It supports adding a task from the words you type, removing a task by its 1-based number, showing the numbered list, and printing a usage message for anything else, including missing or invalid input. Each add or done command saves the file and then prints the updated list, but any failure to read the file is silently treated as an empty list, so a later add could overwrite existing tasks, and the program doesn't say what happens when you complete a number beyond the end of the list.

This is a command-line to-do tool that keeps one task per line in a file named todo.txt in the current directory, treating a missing file as an empty list. Run it with `add` followed by the task words to append a task, `done` followed by a 1-based number to delete that task from the list (it removes the task rather than marking it complete), or `show` to list the numbered tasks; after an add or done it saves the file and prints the updated list. Anything else, including no arguments or a malformed number, prints a usage line, and the program needs permission to read and write files, read arguments, and print to the console, with file write failures reported as errors.

This command-line tool keeps a to-do list in a file named todo.txt in the current directory. It runs one command per invocation: add a task (all remaining words become the task text), mark a numbered task done by removing it, or show the list. After an add or a done it saves the file and prints the numbered list, and any missing, unrecognized or malformed input, including a number below 1 or one that isn't a number, prints a usage message instead. A missing file counts as an empty list and blank lines are ignored. The program only touches the console, command-line arguments and the filesystem, but the code doesn't say what happens when you mark done a number larger than the list, so test that case before relying on it.
